newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Products Outlook-High stocks pressure prices.
newsitem.headline: Asia Products Outlook-High stocks pressure prices.

text.p: Asian naphtha, jet fuel and gas oil prices are under downward pressure as stocks remained plentiful but regional demand was poor, traders said on Monday.
They said even though the market is entering its traditional peak winter demand season, high stocks were reported at storage terminals in most major locations as buyers remained at bay.

The exceptionally high stocks came about as oil companies geared up for the traditional winter play, where the high forward prices on the swaps market more than pays for the cost of storing the product.

However, tank-space is running out and some companies are being forced to offload part of their jet fuel and gas oil on the prompt market to make room for new output or fresh cargoes arriving from the Middle East.
Such moves to ease storage tightness have partly yielded success as latest stock figures showed, but the absolute levels are still high, traders said.

For the week ended August 14, Singapore's Trade Development Board (TDB) reported that middle distillate stocks fell 816,000 barrels to 10.231 million, while light distillates lost 624,000 million barrels to 6.457 million.
Gas oil cargoes were offered in Singapore at up to 30 cents below prevailing spot prices but buyers were still not enticed to pick the barrels.

On a fixed price basis, a European major bought gas oil from a Singapore trader on Friday down to an intra-week low of $22.40 per barrel on a free-on-board Singapore basis, 10 cents below its last traded level on Monday.
Traders said the daily emergence of up to five sellers for both gas oil and jet fuel last week is expected to extend to this week as regional demand remained weak.
"The winter demand has not kicked in yet," one trader said. "Most people have high stocks, including the endusers."
Traders said the shutdown of several refineries in Asia and the Middle East are expected to have minimal impact due to the ample stocks.

Planned maintenance at oil refineries will take about 1.1 million barrels per day (bpd) of capacity out of operation during August and September in the Middle East and Asia, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said earlier.
The production loss will be sharply lower in October to about 700,000-bpd as the maintenance season in the region comes to an end as the industry gears up for winter.

Among the major shutdowns is that of a 100,000-bpd crude unit at Indonesia's Cilacap refinery for 35 days beginning August 12, and the 265,000-bpd unit at Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura refinery for 30 days beginning August 20.
Naphtha prices are similarly depressed.
"The Japanese have increased their domestic production of naphtha and have no need to import," said a Japanese trader.
"In fact some are trying to defer their term liftings from the Middle East."

Imports by Thailand, which caused a bull run in July, are also unlikely to re-emerge as the chemical company the led the charge is no longer in need of naphtha after repairing a damaged unit at its plant.

Aromatics (Thailand) Plc is now able to use condensate as feedstock for its petrochemical plant after the mercury extraction unit was fixed with the plant coming back onstream on August 12, a source said.
The company needs to import at least one cargo per month but had already covered its September demand.
Only Taiwan's state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp (CPC) was an active buyer, seeking 30,000 tonnes of full-range naphtha for October 1-31 delivery in a tender which closes on August 20.

With the softer market, traders expect lower offers than CPC's last full-range naphtha tender, for September 1-10 delivery, which was awarded to South Korean refiner Yukong Ltd at $203 a tonne, on a cost-and-freight (c-and-f) basis.
In the absence of buyers, Singapore refiners were not actively offering September cargoes, although some lifting schedules will only be confirmed this week.
Traders assessed premiums at flat to a "small premium' after an oil major sold a full cargo earlier this month at parity to Singapore spot quotes.
"If you can get flat, you are lucky," said one U.S. major.
Indonesia was adding to the already over-supplied market with a very prompt 200,000-barrel cargo of full range naphtha, lifting August 18-22, which was heard being offered from Dumai.
Some steam was let out of fuel oil's week-long rally on Friday and the market is not expected to chalk up such a big jumps this week, traders said.
At its height, fuel oil swaps rose by about $5.00 per tonne during the week before easing on Friday as the market came under strong selling pressure amid profit taking.
